story: In November 1973, NASA launched Skylab 4 with an all-rookie crew: Gerald Carr, Edward Gibson, and William Pogue. Shortly after reaching orbit, Pogue suffered space sickness. Fearing mission delays, the crew concealed his illness, earning a harsh radio reprimand from Astronaut Office chief Alan Shepard. NASA then pushed the inexperienced crew with a relentless, minute-by-minute schedule. Exhausted and falling behind, the crew accidentally missed a daily radio briefing, causing a 90-minute communications blackout over an entire orbit. Sensational media reports soon claimed the astronauts had staged the first mutiny in space by turning off their radios. In reality, no strike occurred. On December 30, 1973, the crew held a frank radio conference with Capcom Richard Truly to negotiate a manageable pace. NASA relaxed the schedule, and crew productivity soared. The astronauts completed their record-breaking 84-day mission successfully, though none of the three ever flew in space again.
angle: The famous 'mutiny in space' was actually a urban legend caused by an exhausted, all-rookie crew accidentally missing a single 90-minute radio briefing.

claims.claim: Skylab 4 was the third and final crewed mission to the Skylab space station.
The Skylab 4 crew consisted of astronauts Gerald Carr, Edward Gibson, and William Pogue.
All three crew members on Skylab 4 were rookies making their first spaceflight.
Pilot William Pogue suffered from space motion sickness shortly after arriving in orbit.
The crew attempted to hide Pogue's initial space sickness from mission control flight surgeons.
Astronaut Office chief Alan Shepard reprimanded the crew over the radio for concealing the illness.
Mission planners assigned the rookie crew an overburdened and dense work schedule from the start of the flight.
The crew suffered severe fatigue and fell behind schedule while attempting to keep up with ground demands.
The crew missed a scheduled radio briefing, resulting in a loss of communication for one complete orbit of about 90 minutes.
Media reports and popular stories claimed the astronauts went on a strike or mutiny in space by turning off their radios.
NASA and the astronauts confirmed that no intentional strike or mutiny ever took place.
On December 30, 1973, the crew held a radio conference with capsule communicator Richard Truly to adjust their schedule.
NASA agreed to give the crew a more relaxed schedule, which dramatically increased their overall productivity.
The Skylab 4 mission lasted a total of 84 days in space.
None of the three Skylab 4 crew members ever flew in space again after returning to Earth.
The myth of the space strike was widely popularized by a 1976 New Yorker article written by Henry S. F. Cooper.
Lessons learned from the Skylab 4 scheduling friction reshaped future NASA crew selection and mission planning policies.
The crew performed spacewalks to observe and photograph Comet Kohoutek.

disputed: Media accounts and business case studies reported that the crew staged an intentional strike or mutiny by turning off radios; script should present this as an urban legend and clarify it was an accidental missed briefing.

Accounts differ on whether the missed communication resulted from crossed signals among fatigued astronauts or confusion surrounding scheduled days off and ground equipment failures; script should attribute the incident to fatigue and miscommunication rather than deliberate revolt.
